title: Zahlen: null bis hundert
summary: Numbers 0–100 and the reversed-units trick — German says the ones before the tens, all as one word

blocks.title: Zahlen 0–12: die Basis
blocks.body: The numbers 0–10 are simple vocabulary — learn them like any other words. Two look almost regular but aren't: **11** is *elf*, **12** is *zwölf* (not *einzehn*, not *zweizehn*). Get these twelve solid and the rest of the system builds itself.

blocks.title: 13 bis 100: der Zahlendreher
blocks.body: From 13–19, add **-zehn**: *dreizehn, vierzehn, fünfzehn* — but *sechzehn* (one *s*) and *siebzehn* (drops *-en*) contract a little. The tens: **zwanzig** (20) and **dreißig** (30, note the *ß*) are irregular; then it's regular *-zig*: *vierzig, fünfzig, sechzig, siebzig, achtzig, neunzig*, then *hundert*. Now the twist: from 21 on, German says the **ones before the tens**, joined by *und*, as **one word**: **21 = einundzwanzig** — literally "one-and-twenty". *eins* drops its final *-s* here: *ein*undzwanzig, not *einsundzwanzig*.

pairs.note: German swaps the order: ones first, then tens, glued into one word.
Both contract a little: sech(s)zehn, sieb(en)zehn — the base number loses a letter or two.
Both irregular — learn them as their own words, not a formula.

blocks.explain: German gives the ones before the tens: drei-und-vierzig = "three-and-forty" = 43.

blocks.hint: fünfzig (50) + sechs (6) — ones first, one word.
blocks.explain: 56 = sechsundfünfzig — six-and-fifty, glued into one word.

blocks.prompt: Listen and type the number you hear.

blocks.title: Sag dein Alter
blocks.prompt: Complete the sentence: Ich bin ___ Jahre alt.
Numbers day! Write out your age, a made-up phone-style number, and one number between 60 and 99 — all fully in German words.
